extraction_notes.note: The forward search of Section 6.1 repeats Section 5.1 almost word for word (only 'second' vs 'third step' differs); by the one-node-per-repeated-statement rule only the Section 5.1 copy is a node, and the SSD algorithm AP15 uses it. The definition of the index value theta(v) and its rank-order claim are likewise repeated in Sections 5 and 6 and kept once (DP22, ClP8).
The shortcut-construction procedure is described twice, as an overview (Section 3.1) and as a four-step iteration (Section 4); they differ in detail, so both are kept, linked by a specializes edge.
The appendix states Propositions 1-3 as bold items in an itemize list, not as environments; typed proposition because the paper names them so.

The proof of Theorem 1 is the whole appendix; the proof node is only the sentence combining the three propositions, and the propositions and their prose proofs are separate top-level nodes with uses edges into it.

The appendix proofs contain typos: an undefined $e_3$ in Proposition 2's proof, and in Proposition 3's proof a missing \rangle, '$v_1 = v_x$' for $v_y$, and '$P_1^*$' where $P_3^*$ is meant. Statements are copied verbatim.

nodes.name: Highways-on-Disk (HoD)
nodes.statement: To address the deficiency of existing work, this paper proposes {\em Highways-on-Disk (HoD)}, a disk-based index that supports both SSD and SSSP queries on directed and weighted graphs. The key idea of HoD is to augment the input graph with a set of auxiliary edges (referred to as {\em shortcuts} \cite{ss05}), and exploit them during query processing to reduce I/O and computation costs.
differentia: supports both SSD and SSSP queries on directed and weighted graphs
nodes.statement_short: HoD: disk-based index for SSD/SSSP queries on directed weighted graphs, augmenting the graph with shortcut edges.

nodes.name: Shortcut
nodes.statement: Each shortcut has the same length with the shortest path connecting the endpoints of the shortcut.

nodes.name: Dijkstra's algorithm
nodes.statement: The classic solution for SSD and SSSP queries is Dijkstra's algorithm \cite{d59}. Given a SSD or SSSP query from a node $s$, Dijkstra's algorithm traverses the graph starting from $s$, such that the nodes in $G$ are visited in ascending order of their distances from $s$. Once a node $v$ is visited, the algorithm returns the distance from $s$ to $v$ based on the information maintained during the traversal; the shortest path from $s$ to $v$ can also be efficiently derived if required.
nodes.statement_short: Traverse the graph from $s$ visiting nodes in ascending distance order, reporting each node's distance when visited.

nodes.name: Traverse in distance order
nodes.statement: Given a SSD or SSSP query from a node $s$, Dijkstra's algorithm traverses the graph starting from $s$, such that the nodes in $G$ are visited in ascending order of their distances from $s$.
nodes.statement_short: Traverse from $s$ in ascending distance order

nodes.name: Report distance on visit
nodes.statement: Once a node $v$ is visited, the algorithm returns the distance from $s$ to $v$ based on the information maintained during the traversal; the shortest path from $s$ to $v$ can also be efficiently derived if required.
nodes.statement_short: Return the distance of each visited node

nodes.name: VC-Index
nodes.statement: The basic idea of VC-Index is to pre-compute a number of {\em reduced} versions of the input graph $G$. Each reduced graph contains some relatively important nodes in $G$, as well as the distances between some pairs of those nodes. During query processing, VC-Index scans a selected subset of reduced graphs, and then derives query results based on the pre-computed distances.
nodes.statement_short: Prior disk-based index: precompute reduced graphs with pairwise distances, then answer queries by scanning a subset of them.

nodes.name: Precompute reduced graphs
nodes.statement: The basic idea of VC-Index is to pre-compute a number of {\em reduced} versions of the input graph $G$. Each reduced graph contains some relatively important nodes in $G$, as well as the distances between some pairs of those nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Precompute reduced graphs holding important nodes and distances

nodes.name: Scan reduced graphs at query time
nodes.statement: During query processing, VC-Index scans a selected subset of reduced graphs, and then derives query results based on the pre-computed distances.
nodes.statement_short: Scan selected reduced graphs and derive results

nodes.name: Weighted directed graph $G$
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a weighted and directed graph with a set $V$ of nodes and a set $E$ of edges.

nodes.name: Edge length
nodes.statement: Each edge $e$ in $E$ is associated with a positive weight $l(e)$, which is referred to as the {\em length} of $e$.

nodes.name: Path
nodes.statement: A path $P$ in $G$ is a sequence of nodes $\langle v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k \rangle$, such that $\langle v_i, v_{i+1}\rangle$ ($i \in [1, k-1]$) is a directed edge in $G$.
differentia: $\langle v_i, v_{i+1}\rangle$ ($i \in [1, k-1]$) is a directed edge in $G$

nodes.name: Path length
nodes.statement: The length of $P$ is defined as the sum of the length of each edge on $P$.

nodes.name: Notation $l(e)$, $l(P)$
nodes.statement: We use $l(e)$ and $l(P)$ to denote the length of an edge $e$ and a path $P$, respectively.

nodes.name: Distance $dist(s,t)$
nodes.statement: For any two nodes $s$ and $t$ in $G$, we define the {\em distance} from $s$ to $t$, denoted as $dist(s, t)$, as the length of the shortest path from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.genus: the length of the shortest path from $s$ to $t$

nodes.name: Single-source distance (SSD) query
nodes.statement: Given a {\em source node} $s$ in $G$, a {\em single-source distance (SSD)} query asks for the distance from $s$ to any other node in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Given source $s$, return $dist(s,v)$ for every node $v$.

nodes.name: Single-source shortest path (SSSP) query
nodes.statement: Meanwhile, a {\em single-source shortest path (SSSP)} query from $s$ retrieves not only the distance from $s$ to any other node $v$, but also the {\em predecessor} of $v$, i.e., the node that immediately precedes $v$ in the shortest path from $s$ to $v$.
nodes.statement_short: Given source $s$, return for every $v$ its distance and its predecessor on the shortest $s$-$v$ path.

nodes.name: Memory size $M$ and block size $B$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be the size of the main memory available, and $B$ be the size of a disk block, both measured in the number of words.

nodes.name: Semi-external memory assumption
nodes.statement: We assume that $B \le |V| \le M \le |E|$, i.e., the main memory can accommodate all nodes but not all edges in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Memory holds all nodes but not all edges: $B \le |V| \le M \le |E|$.

nodes.name: Disk-based index for SSD/SSSP queries
nodes.statement: Our objective is to devise an index structure on $G$ that answers any SSD or SSSP query with small I/O and CPU costs, such that the index requires at most $M$ main memory in pre-computation and query processing.
nodes.statement_short: Design an index answering SSD/SSSP queries with small I/O and CPU cost using at most $M$ memory.

nodes.name: HoD iterative shortcut construction (overview)
nodes.statement: In a nut shell, HoD constructs shortcuts with an iterative procedure, which takes as input a copy of the graph $G$ (denoted as $G_0$). In the $i$-th ($i \ge 1$) iteration of the procedure, HoD first {\em reduces} $G_{i-1}$ by removing a selected set of {\em less important} nodes in $G_{i-1}$, and then, it constructs shortcuts in the reduced graph to ensure that the distance between any two remaining nodes is not affected by the node removal. The resulting graph (with shortcuts added) is denoted as $G_i$, and it is fed as the input of the ($i{+}1$)-th iteration of procedure. This procedure terminates only when the reduced graph $G_i$ is {\em sufficiently small}. All shortcuts created during the procedure are inserted into the original graph $G$, leading to an augmented graph $G^*$ that would be used by HoD for query processing.
input: a copy of the graph $G$ (denoted as $G_0$)
nodes.statement_short: Iteratively remove less important nodes and add shortcuts preserving distances, until the reduced graph is small; collect shortcuts into $G^*$.

nodes.name: Remove less important nodes
nodes.statement: In the $i$-th ($i \ge 1$) iteration of the procedure, HoD first {\em reduces} $G_{i-1}$ by removing a selected set of {\em less important} nodes in $G_{i-1}$, and then, it constructs shortcuts in the reduced graph to ensure that the distance between any two remaining nodes is not affected by the node removal.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $G_{i-1}$ and add distance-preserving shortcuts

nodes.name: Feed next iteration
nodes.statement: The resulting graph (with shortcuts added) is denoted as $G_i$, and it is fed as the input of the ($i{+}1$)-th iteration of procedure.
nodes.statement_short: Pass $G_i$ to the next iteration

nodes.name: Terminate when small
nodes.statement: This procedure terminates only when the reduced graph $G_i$ is {\em sufficiently small}.
nodes.statement_short: Stop once the reduced graph is sufficiently small

nodes.name: Build augmented graph
nodes.statement: All shortcuts created during the procedure are inserted into the original graph $G$, leading to an augmented graph $G^*$ that would be used by HoD for query processing.
nodes.statement_short: Insert all shortcuts into $G$ to obtain $G^*$

nodes.name: Example 1 (graph reduction and shortcut construction)
nodes.statement: \em Assume that the input to the iterative procedure is the graph $G_0$ in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}a. Further assume that the reduced graph is sufficiently small if it contains at most two nodes and two edges. In the first iteration of the procedure, HoD inspects $G_0$ and identifies $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3$ as less important nodes. To explain, observe that the node $v_1$ in $G_0$ does not have any incoming edge, while $v_2$ and $v_3$ have no outgoing edges. As a consequence, $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3$ do not lie on the shortest path between any two other nodes. That is, even if we remove $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3$ from $G_0$, the distance between any two remaining nodes is not affected. Intuitively, this indicates that $v_1$, $v_2$, $v_3$ are of little importance for SSD queries. Therefore, HoD eliminates $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3$ from $G_0$, which results in the reduced graph $G_1$ in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}b. \vspace{0mm} In the second iteration, HoD selects $v_4$, $v_5$, and $v_6$ as the less important nodes in $G_1$, and removes them from $G_1$. The removal of $v_4$ changes the distance from $v_8$ to $v_9$ to $+\infty$, since $\langle v_8, v_4, v_9\rangle$ is the only path (in $G_1$) that starts at $v_8$ and ends at $v_9$. To mitigate this change, HoD inserts into $G_1$ a shortcut $\langle v_8, v_9\rangle$ that has the same length with $\langle v_8, v_4, v_9\rangle$, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}c. As such, the distance between any two nodes in $G_1$ remains unchanged after $v_4$ is removed. Similarly, when HoD eliminates $v_6$, it constructs a shortcut $\langle v_9, v_7\rangle$ with a length $2$ to reconnect the two neighbors of $v_6$. Meanwhile, $v_5$ is removed without creating any shortcut, since deleting $v_5$ does not change the distance between its two neighbors. Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}c illustrates the resulting reduced graph $G_2$. To explain why HoD chooses to remove $v_4$, $v_5$, and $v_6$ from $G_1$, observe that each of those nodes has only two neighbors. For any of such nodes, even if the removal of the node changes the distance between its neighbors, HoD only needs to construct one shortcut to reconnect its neighbors. In other words, the number of shortcuts required is minimum, which helps reduce the space consumption of HoD. In contrast, if HoD chooses to remove $v_9$ from $G_1$ (which has a larger number of neighbors than $v_4$, $v_5$, and $v_6$), then much more shortcuts would need to be constructed. \vspace{0mm} Finally, in the third iteration, HoD removes $v_7$ and $v_8$ from $G_2$ as they are considered unimportant. The removal of $v_7$ leads to a new shortcut $\langle v_9, v_{10}\rangle$ with a length $3$, since $\langle v_9, v_7, v_{10}\rangle$ is the only path connecting $v_9$ to $v_{10}$, and the length of the path equals $3$. On the other hand, $v_8$ is directly eliminated as it is not on the shortest path between its only two neighbors $v_9$ and $v_{10}$. Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}d shows the reduced graph $G_3$ after the removal of $v_7$ and $v_8$. Assume that the reduced graph $G_3$ is considered sufficiently small by HoD. Then, the iterative procedure of HoD would terminate. The three shortcuts created during the procedure (i.e., $\langle v_8, v_9\rangle$, $\langle v_9, v_7 \rangle$, and $\langle v_9, v_{10}\rangle$) are added into the original graph $G$, which leads to the augmented graph $G^*$ in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}d. \hspace*{\fill} {$\square$}
nodes.statement_short: Three reduction iterations on a 10-node graph produce shortcuts $\langle v_8,v_9\rangle$, $\langle v_9,v_7\rangle$, $\langle v_9,v_{10}\rangle$.
nodes.label: example:over-steps

nodes.name: Core graph $G_c$
nodes.statement: We use $G_c$ to denote this memory-resident reduced graph, and we refer to it as the {\em core graph}.

nodes.name: Rank $r(v)$
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the {\em rank} $r(v)$ of each node $v$ in $G$ as follows: \begin{enumerate} [itemsep = 0.5mm, topsep = 2mm] \item If $v$ is removed in the $i$-th iteration of the iterative procedure, then $r(v) = i$; \item If $v$ is not removed in any iteration (i.e., $v$ is retained in the core graph $G_c$), then $r(v) = 1 + \max_{v \notin G_c} r(v)$, i.e., $r(v)$ is larger than the maximum rank of any node not in $G_c$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $r(v)=i$ if $v$ is removed in iteration $i$; core-graph nodes get rank one more than the maximum rank of removed nodes.

nodes.name: Ranks in Example 1
nodes.statement: For instance, in Example~\ref{example:over-steps}, the ranks of $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3$ equal $1$, since they are removed from $G$ in the first iteration of the reduction procedure. Similarly, $r(v_4) = r(v_5) = r(v_6) = 2$, and $r(v_7) = r(v_8) = 3$. The ranks of $v_9$ and $v_{10}$ equal $4$, since they are in the core graph $G_c$.

nodes.name: HoD SSD query processing (overview)
nodes.statement: Given an SSD query from a node $s$, HoD answers the query with two traversals of the augmented graph $G^*$. The first traversal starts from $s$, and it follows only the {\em outgoing} edges of each node, ignoring any edge {\em whose starting point ranks higher than the ending point}. For instance, if HoD traverses from the node $v_9$ in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}e, it would ignore the outgoing edge $\langle v_9, v_7\rangle$, since $r(v_9) = 4 > r(v_7) = 3$. As such, the first traversal of HoD never moves from a high-rank node to a low-rank node, and it terminates only when no higher-rank nodes can be reached. For each node $v$ visited, HoD maintains the distance from $s$ to $v$ along the paths that have been seen during the traversal, denoted as $dist(s, v)$. Let $V'$ be the set of nodes that are not in the core graph of $G^*$. The second traversal of HoD is performed as a linear scan of the nodes in $V'$, {\em in descending order of their ranks}. For each node $v' \in V'$ scanned, HoD inspects each {\em incoming} edge $e$ of $v'$, and then checks the starting point $u$ of the edge. For any such $u$, HoD calculates $dist(s, u) + l(e)$ as an upperbound of the distance from $s$ to $v'$. (Our solution guarantees that $u$ should have been visited by HoD before $v'$.) Once all incoming edges of $v'$ are inspected, HoD derives the distance from $s$ to $v'$ based on the upperbounds, and then it moves on to the next node in $V'$. This process terminates when all nodes in $V'$ are examined.
input: an SSD query from a node $s$
nodes.statement_short: Upward traversal from $s$ along rank-increasing edges, then a linear scan of non-core nodes in descending rank relaxing incoming edges.

nodes.name: First (upward) traversal
nodes.statement: The first traversal starts from $s$, and it follows only the {\em outgoing} edges of each node, ignoring any edge {\em whose starting point ranks higher than the ending point}. For instance, if HoD traverses from the node $v_9$ in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}e, it would ignore the outgoing edge $\langle v_9, v_7\rangle$, since $r(v_9) = 4 > r(v_7) = 3$. As such, the first traversal of HoD never moves from a high-rank node to a low-rank node, and it terminates only when no higher-rank nodes can be reached.
nodes.statement_short: Traverse from $s$ only along edges to higher-rank nodes

nodes.name: Maintain tentative distances
nodes.statement: For each node $v$ visited, HoD maintains the distance from $s$ to $v$ along the paths that have been seen during the traversal, denoted as $dist(s, v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Keep best-seen distance for visited nodes

nodes.name: Second traversal: descending-rank scan
nodes.statement: Let $V'$ be the set of nodes that are not in the core graph of $G^*$. The second traversal of HoD is performed as a linear scan of the nodes in $V'$, {\em in descending order of their ranks}. For each node $v' \in V'$ scanned, HoD inspects each {\em incoming} edge $e$ of $v'$, and then checks the starting point $u$ of the edge. For any such $u$, HoD calculates $dist(s, u) + l(e)$ as an upperbound of the distance from $s$ to $v'$. (Our solution guarantees that $u$ should have been visited by HoD before $v'$.) Once all incoming edges of $v'$ are inspected, HoD derives the distance from $s$ to $v'$ based on the upperbounds, and then it moves on to the next node in $V'$. This process terminates when all nodes in $V'$ are examined.
nodes.statement_short: Scan non-core nodes in descending rank, bounding distance via incoming edges

nodes.name: Rank-ordered traversal property
nodes.statement: The query algorithm of HoD has an interesting property: the first traversal of the algorithm always visits nodes in ascending order of their ranks (as it never follows an edge that connects a high-rank node to low-rank node), while the second phase always visits nodes in descending rank order. Intuitively, if we maintain two copies of the augmented graph, such that the first (resp.\ second) copy stores nodes in ascending (resp.\ descending) order of their ranks, then HoD can answer any SSD query with a linear scan of the two copies. This leads to high query efficiency as it avoids random disk accesses.
nodes.statement_short: First traversal visits nodes in ascending rank, second in descending rank, so storing two rank-ordered copies enables linear scans.

nodes.name: HoD preprocessing iteration
nodes.statement: As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:overview-pre}, the preprocessing algorithm of HoD takes as input a copy $G_0$ of the graph $G$, and it iteratively reduces $G_0$ into smaller graphs $G_1, G_2, \ldots$, during which it creates shortcuts to augment $G$. More specifically, the ($i{+}1$)-th ($i \ge 0$) iteration of the algorithm has four steps: \begin{enumerate} [itemsep = 0.5mm, topsep = 2mm] \item Select a set $R_i$ of nodes to be removed from $G_{i}$. \item For each node $v \in R_i$, construct shortcuts in $G_{i}$ to ensure that the removal of $v$ does not change the distance between any two remaining nodes. \item Remove the nodes in $R_i$ from $G_{i}$ to obtain a further reduced graph $G_{i+1}$. Store information about the removed nodes in the index file of HoD. \item Pass the $G_{i+1}$ to the ($i{+}2$)-th iteration as input. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Each iteration selects removal set $R_i$, adds shortcuts, removes $R_i$ writing removed nodes to the index, and passes $G_{i+1}$ on.

nodes.name: Select removal set
nodes.statement: Select a set $R_i$ of nodes to be removed from $G_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose nodes $R_i$ to remove

nodes.name: Construct shortcuts
nodes.statement: For each node $v \in R_i$, construct shortcuts in $G_{i}$ to ensure that the removal of $v$ does not change the distance between any two remaining nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Add distance-preserving shortcuts for each removed node

nodes.name: Remove nodes and store
nodes.statement: Remove the nodes in $R_i$ from $G_{i}$ to obtain a further reduced graph $G_{i+1}$. Store information about the removed nodes in the index file of HoD.
nodes.statement_short: Remove $R_i$ and store their info in the index

nodes.name: Pass to next iteration
nodes.statement: Pass the $G_{i+1}$ to the ($i{+}2$)-th iteration as input.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate on $G_{i+1}$

nodes.name: Edge triplet representation
nodes.statement: For ease of exposition, we represent each edge $e = \langle u, v \rangle$ as a triplet $\left\langle u, v, l(e)\right\rangle$ or $\left\langle v, u, -l(e)\right\rangle$, where $l(e)$ is the length of $e$. For example, the edge $\langle v_9, v_7 \rangle$ in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}a can be represented as either $\left\langle v_9, v_7, 2\right\rangle$ or $\left\langle v_7, v_9, -2\right\rangle$. That is, a negative length in the triplet indicates that the second node in the triplet is the starting point of the edge.

nodes.name: Adjacency-list disk layout
nodes.statement: In addition, we assume that the input graph $G$ is stored on the disk as adjacency lists, such that (i) for any two nodes $v_i$ and $v_j$, the adjacency list of $v_i$ precedes that of $v_j$ if $i < j$, and (ii) each edge $\langle v_i, v_j\rangle$ with length $l$ is stored twice: once in the adjacency list of $v_i$ (as a triplet $\langle v_i, v_j, l\rangle$), and another in the adjacency list of $v_j$ (as a triplet $\langle v_j, v_i, -l\rangle$).
nodes.statement_short: Graph stored as id-ordered adjacency lists with each edge stored twice, as outgoing and incoming triplet.

nodes.name: Node $v^*$ to be removed
nodes.statement: Let $v^*$ be a node to be removed from $G_{i}$.

nodes.name: Outgoing neighbor
nodes.statement: We define an {\em outgoing neighbor} of $v^*$ as a node $u$ to which $v^*$ has an outgoing edge.

nodes.name: Incoming neighbor
nodes.statement: Similarly, an {\em incoming neighbor} of $v^*$ is a node $w$ from which $v^*$ has an incoming edge.

nodes.name: Observation 1 (distance change under node removal)
nodes.statement: \em For any two nodes $v_j$ and $v_k$ in $G_i$, the distance from $v_j$ to $v_k$ changes after $v^*$ is removed, if and only if the shortest path from $v_j$ to $v_k$ contains a sub-path $\langle u, v^*, w\rangle$, such that $u$ (resp.\ $w$) is an incoming (resp.\ outgoing) neighbor of $v^*$. \hspace*{\fill} {$\square$}
assumptions: For any two nodes $v_j$ and $v_k$ in $G_i$
conclusions: the distance from $v_j$ to $v_k$ changes after $v^*$ is removed, if and only if the shortest path from $v_j$ to $v_k$ contains a sub-path $\langle u, v^*, w\rangle$, such that $u$ (resp.\ $w$) is an incoming (resp.\ outgoing) neighbor of $v^*$
nodes.statement_short: Removing $v^*$ changes a distance iff the shortest path passes through $v^*$ from an in-neighbor to an out-neighbor.
nodes.label: observ:pre-neighbor

nodes.name: Redundant shortcut criterion
nodes.statement: In general, for any incoming neighbor $u$ and outgoing neighbor $w$ of $v^*$, a shortcut from $u$ to $w$ is unnecessary if there is a path $P$ from $u$ to $v$, such that (i) $P$ does not go through $v^*$, and (ii) $P$ is no longer than $\langle u, v^*, w\rangle$.
assumptions: for any incoming neighbor $u$ and outgoing neighbor $w$ of $v^*$
there is a path $P$ from $u$ to $v$, such that (i) $P$ does not go through $v^*$, and (ii) $P$ is no longer than $\langle u, v^*, w\rangle$
conclusions: a shortcut from $u$ to $w$ is unnecessary

nodes.name: Shortcut generation via candidate and baseline edges
nodes.statement: Specifically, for each $v^*$ in the node set $R_i$ to be removed from $G_i$, we generate a {\em candidate edge} $e_c = \langle u, w\rangle$ from each incoming neighbor $u$ of $v^*$ to each outgoing neighbor $w$ of $v^*$, setting the length of the shortcut to $l(\langle u, v^*, w\rangle)$. For any such candidate edge $e_c$, we insert it into a temporary file $T$ as two triplets: $\langle u, w, l(e_c)\rangle$ and $\langle w, u, -l(e_c)\rangle$. In addition to the candidate edges, we also insert two additional groups of edges (referred to as {\em baseline edges}) into the temporary file $T$ as triplets. The first group consists of any edge $e$ in $G_i$ connecting two nodes not in $R_i$, i.e., the two endpoints of $e$ are not to be removed. The second group is generated as follows: for each node $v$ not in $R_i$, we select $v$'s certain incoming neighbor $u'$ and outgoing neighbor $w'$, and we construct a baseline edge $\langle u', w'\rangle$, setting its length to $l(\langle u', v, w'\rangle)$. The purpose of inserting a baseline edge $e$ into the temporary file $T$ is to help eliminate any redundant candidate edge that (i) shares the same endpoints with $e$ but (ii) is not shorter than $e$. Towards this end, once all baseline edges are added into $T$, we sort the triplets in $T$ using a standard algorithm for external sort, such that a triplet $t_1 = \langle v_a, v_b, l_1\rangle$ precedes another triplet $t_2 = \langle v_\alpha, v_\beta, l_2\rangle$, if any of the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} [itemsep = 0.5mm, topsep = 2mm] \item $a < \alpha$, or $a = \alpha$ but $b < \beta$. \item $a = \alpha$, $b = \beta$, and $l_1 > 0 > l_2$. That is, any outgoing edge of a node precedes its incoming edges. \item $a = \alpha$, $b = \beta$, $l_1 \cdot l_2 > 0$ (i.e., $t_1$ and $t_2$ are both incoming edges or both outgoing edges), and $|l_1| < |l_2|$. That is, $t_1$ and $t_2$ share the same starting and ending points, but $t_1$ is shorter than $t_2$. \item $a = \alpha$, $b = \beta$, $l_1 \cdot l_2 > 0$, $|l_1| = |l_2|$, and $t_1$ is a baseline edge while $t_2$ is a candidate edge. \end{enumerate} Once $T$ is sorted, the outgoing (resp.\ incoming) edges with the same endpoints are grouped together, and the first edge in each group should have the smallest length within the group. If the first edge $e$ in a group is a candidate edge, then we retain $e$ as it is shorter than any other baseline or candidate edges that we have generated. On the other hand, if $e$ is a baseline edge, then the distance between the endpoints of $e$ must not be affected by the removal of any nodes in $R_i$. In that case, all candidate edges in the group can be omitted. With one linear scan of the sorted $T$ and the adjacency lists of $G_i$, we can remove the information of any node in $R_i$, and merge the retained candidate edges into the adjacency lists of the remaining nodes.
input: each $v^*$ in the node set $R_i$ to be removed from $G_i$
nodes.statement_short: Write candidate and baseline edge triplets to a temp file, external-sort them, keep a candidate only if it is the shortest in its group, then merge.

nodes.statement_short: For removed $v^*$, an edge from each in-neighbor $u$ to each out-neighbor $w$ with length $l(\langle u,v^*,w\rangle)$.

nodes.name: Generate candidate edges
nodes.statement: Specifically, for each $v^*$ in the node set $R_i$ to be removed from $G_i$, we generate a {\em candidate edge} $e_c = \langle u, w\rangle$ from each incoming neighbor $u$ of $v^*$ to each outgoing neighbor $w$ of $v^*$, setting the length of the shortcut to $l(\langle u, v^*, w\rangle)$. For any such candidate edge $e_c$, we insert it into a temporary file $T$ as two triplets: $\langle u, w, l(e_c)\rangle$ and $\langle w, u, -l(e_c)\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Generate candidate edges and write them to $T$

nodes.name: Insert baseline edges
nodes.statement: In addition to the candidate edges, we also insert two additional groups of edges (referred to as {\em baseline edges}) into the temporary file $T$ as triplets. The first group consists of any edge $e$ in $G_i$ connecting two nodes not in $R_i$, i.e., the two endpoints of $e$ are not to be removed. The second group is generated as follows: for each node $v$ not in $R_i$, we select $v$'s certain incoming neighbor $u'$ and outgoing neighbor $w'$, and we construct a baseline edge $\langle u', w'\rangle$, setting its length to $l(\langle u', v, w'\rangle)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write baseline edges (kept edges and some two-hop paths) to $T$

nodes.name: External sort of triplets
nodes.statement: The purpose of inserting a baseline edge $e$ into the temporary file $T$ is to help eliminate any redundant candidate edge that (i) shares the same endpoints with $e$ but (ii) is not shorter than $e$. Towards this end, once all baseline edges are added into $T$, we sort the triplets in $T$ using a standard algorithm for external sort, such that a triplet $t_1 = \langle v_a, v_b, l_1\rangle$ precedes another triplet $t_2 = \langle v_\alpha, v_\beta, l_2\rangle$, if any of the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} [itemsep = 0.5mm, topsep = 2mm] \item $a < \alpha$, or $a = \alpha$ but $b < \beta$. \item $a = \alpha$, $b = \beta$, and $l_1 > 0 > l_2$. That is, any outgoing edge of a node precedes its incoming edges. \item $a = \alpha$, $b = \beta$, $l_1 \cdot l_2 > 0$ (i.e., $t_1$ and $t_2$ are both incoming edges or both outgoing edges), and $|l_1| < |l_2|$. That is, $t_1$ and $t_2$ share the same starting and ending points, but $t_1$ is shorter than $t_2$. \item $a = \alpha$, $b = \beta$, $l_1 \cdot l_2 > 0$, $|l_1| = |l_2|$, and $t_1$ is a baseline edge while $t_2$ is a candidate edge. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Externally sort $T$ by endpoints, direction, length, baseline-first

nodes.name: Keep shortest candidate per group
nodes.statement: Once $T$ is sorted, the outgoing (resp.\ incoming) edges with the same endpoints are grouped together, and the first edge in each group should have the smallest length within the group. If the first edge $e$ in a group is a candidate edge, then we retain $e$ as it is shorter than any other baseline or candidate edges that we have generated. On the other hand, if $e$ is a baseline edge, then the distance between the endpoints of $e$ must not be affected by the removal of any nodes in $R_i$. In that case, all candidate edges in the group can be omitted.
nodes.statement_short: Retain a candidate only if it heads its group; else drop the group's candidates

nodes.name: Merge into adjacency lists
nodes.statement: With one linear scan of the sorted $T$ and the adjacency lists of $G_i$, we can remove the information of any node in $R_i$, and merge the retained candidate edges into the adjacency lists of the remaining nodes.
nodes.statement_short: One linear scan removes $R_i$ and merges retained shortcuts

nodes.name: Example 3 (node removal and shortcut generation)
nodes.statement: \em Suppose that, given the graph $G_i$ in Figure~\ref{fig:pre-contract}a, we are to remove a node set $R_i = \{v_2, v_4\}$ from $G_i$. $v_2$ has only one incoming neighbor $v_1$ and one outgoing neighbor $v_3$, and $l(\langle v_1, v_2, v_3\rangle) = 2$. Accordingly, HoD generates a candidate edge $\langle v_1, v_3\rangle$ by inserting into the temporary file $T$ two triplets, $\langle v_1, v_3, 2\rangle$ and $\langle v_3, v_1, -2\rangle$. Similarly, for $v_4$, HoD creates a candidate edge $\langle v_1, v_5\rangle$, which is represented as two triplets in $T$: $\langle v_1, v_5, 2\rangle$ and $\langle v_5, v_1, -2\rangle$. Meanwhile, the edge $\langle v_1, v_3\rangle$ in $G_i$ is selected as a baseline edge and is inserted into $T$, since neither $v_1$ nor $v_3$ is in $R_i$. In addition, HoD also generates a baseline edge $\langle v_1, v_5\rangle$ from the neighbors of $v_3$. This is because that (i) $v_1, v_3, v_5$ are not in $R_i$, (ii) $v_1$ is an incoming neighbor of $v_3$, and (iii) $v_5$ is an outgoing neighbor of $v_3$. Figure~\ref{fig:pre-contract}c illustrates the temporary file $T$ after all candidate and baseline edges are inserted, with some triplets omitted for simplicity. Figure~\ref{fig:pre-contract}d shows the file $T$ after it is sorted. The baseline edge $\langle v_1, v_3, 1\rangle$ precedes the candidate edge $\langle v_1, v_3, 2\rangle$, which indicates that we do not need to add a shortcut from $v_1$ to $v_3$. Similarly, the baseline edge $\langle v_3, v_1, -1\rangle$ precedes the candidate edge $\langle v_3, v_1, -2\rangle$, in which case the latter is omitted. Overall, each of the candidate edges in $T$ is preceded by a baseline edge, and hence, no shortcut will be created. Consequently, HoD removes from $G_i$ the adjacency lists of $v_2$ and $v_4$, as well as all edges to and from $v_2$ and $v_4$ in any other adjacency lists. This results in the reduced graph illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:pre-contract}b. \hspace*{\fill} {$\square$}
nodes.statement_short: Removing $\{v_2,v_4\}$: both candidate edges are dominated by baseline edges after sorting, so no shortcut is created.
nodes.label: example:pre-removal

nodes.name: Retained redundant candidates do not affect correctness
nodes.statement: This heuristic approach may retain unnecessary candidate edges, but it does not affect the correctness of SSD queries.
conclusions: it does not affect the correctness of SSD queries
assumptions: This heuristic approach may retain unnecessary candidate edges

nodes.name: Proof that redundant candidates are harmless
nodes.statement: To understand this, recall that each candidate edge $e = \langle u, w\rangle$ has the same length with a certain path $\langle u, v^*, w\rangle$ that {\em exists} in $G_i$, where $v^*$ is the node whose removal leads to the creation of $e$. In other words, the length of $e$ is at least larger than or equal to the distance from $u$ to $w$. Adding such an edge into $G_i$ would not decrease the distance between any two nodes in $G_i$, and hence, retaining $e$ does not change the results of any SSD queries.
nodes.statement_short: A candidate edge has the length of an existing two-hop path, so it is no shorter than the distance and cannot decrease any distance.

nodes.name: Recall candidate length
nodes.statement: To understand this, recall that each candidate edge $e = \langle u, w\rangle$ has the same length with a certain path $\langle u, v^*, w\rangle$ that {\em exists} in $G_i$, where $v^*$ is the node whose removal leads to the creation of $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall each candidate equals an existing two-hop path

nodes.name: Bound candidate length
nodes.statement: In other words, the length of $e$ is at least larger than or equal to the distance from $u$ to $w$.
nodes.statement_short: Candidate length is at least $dist(u,w)$

nodes.name: Conclude no distance changes
nodes.statement: Adding such an edge into $G_i$ would not decrease the distance between any two nodes in $G_i$, and hence, retaining $e$ does not change the results of any SSD queries.
nodes.statement_short: Adding it changes no distances

nodes.name: In/out neighbor sets $B_{in}$, $B_{out}$
nodes.statement: Let $B_{in}$ and $B_{out}$ be the set of incoming and outgoing neighbors of $v$, respectively.

nodes.name: Score $s(v)$ and unimportant node
nodes.statement: The maximum number of shortcuts induced by $v$'s removal is: \begin{equation} s(v) = {\big |}B_{in}{\big |} \cdot {\big |}B_{out} \setminus B_{in}{\big |} + {\big |}B_{out}{\big |} \cdot {\big |}B_{in} \setminus B_{out}{\big |}. \end{equation} We refer to $s(v)$ as the {\em score} of $v$ in $G_i$, and we consider $v$ {\em unimportant} if $s(v)$ is no more than the median score in $G_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Score $s(v)$ is the maximum number of shortcuts $v$'s removal induces; $v$ is unimportant if its score is at most the median.

nodes.name: Node score formula
nodes.statement: s(v) = {\big |}B_{in}{\big |} \cdot {\big |}B_{out} \setminus B_{in}{\big |} + {\big |}B_{out}{\big |} \cdot {\big |}B_{in} \setminus B_{out}{\big |}.
nodes.label: eqn:pre-score

nodes.name: Non-adjacent removal rule
nodes.statement: To avoid the above error, whenever HoD chooses to delete a node $v$ from $G_i$, it will retain all neighbors of $v$ in $G_i$, even if some neighbor might be unimportant.
nodes.statement_short: When a node is removed, all its neighbors are kept in that iteration, so no two adjacent nodes are removed together.

nodes.name: Baseline edge
nodes.statement: As mentioned in Section~\ref{sec:pre-removal}, a baseline edge generated by the preprocessing algorithm of HoD is either (i) an edge in $G_i$ whose endpoints are not to be removed, or (ii) an artificial edge $\langle u, w\rangle$ that corresponds to certain two-hop path $\langle u, v, w\rangle$ in $G_i$, such that none of $u, v, w$ is to be removed.
differentia: an edge in $G_i$ whose endpoints are not to be removed
an artificial edge $\langle u, w\rangle$ that corresponds to certain two-hop path $\langle u, v, w\rangle$ in $G_i$, such that none of $u, v, w$ is to be removed

nodes.name: Sampling two-hop baseline edges
nodes.statement: Therefore, we only select a subset of the two-hop paths in $G_i$ for baseline edge generation. In particular, the total number of two-hop paths selected is set to $c \cdot \sum_{v \in R_i} s(v)$, where $c$ is a small constant, $s(v)$ is as defined in Equation~\ref{eqn:pre-score}, and $\sum_{v \in R_i} s(v)$ is the total number of candidate edges induced by the removal of nodes in $R_i$. In other words, we require that the number of baseline edges generated from two-hop paths is at most $c$ times the number of candidate edges. In our implementation of HoD, we set $c = 5$. Those $c \cdot \sum_{v \in R_i} s(v)$ baseline edges are generated as follows. First, we randomly choose an edge in $G_i$, and arbitrarily select an endpoint $v$ of the edge that is not in $R_i$. (Note that such an endpoint always exists.) After that, from the incoming (resp.\ outgoing) neighbors of $v$, we randomly select a node $u$ (resp.\ $w$), and we generate a baseline edge $\langle u, w\rangle$, setting its length to $l(\langle u, v, w\rangle)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sample $c\sum_{v\in R_i}s(v)$ two-hop paths by picking a random edge, a non-removed endpoint, and random in/out neighbors of it.

nodes.name: Set sampling budget
nodes.statement: In particular, the total number of two-hop paths selected is set to $c \cdot \sum_{v \in R_i} s(v)$, where $c$ is a small constant, $s(v)$ is as defined in Equation~\ref{eqn:pre-score}, and $\sum_{v \in R_i} s(v)$ is the total number of candidate edges induced by the removal of nodes in $R_i$. In other words, we require that the number of baseline edges generated from two-hop paths is at most $c$ times the number of candidate edges. In our implementation of HoD, we set $c = 5$.
nodes.statement_short: Budget: $c$ times the number of candidate edges, $c=5$

nodes.name: Pick random edge endpoint
nodes.statement: First, we randomly choose an edge in $G_i$, and arbitrarily select an endpoint $v$ of the edge that is not in $R_i$. (Note that such an endpoint always exists.)
nodes.statement_short: Pick a random edge and a non-removed endpoint $v$

nodes.name: Generate baseline edge
nodes.statement: After that, from the incoming (resp.\ outgoing) neighbors of $v$, we randomly select a node $u$ (resp.\ $w$), and we generate a baseline edge $\langle u, w\rangle$, setting its length to $l(\langle u, v, w\rangle)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick random in/out neighbors and emit baseline edge

nodes.name: Preprocessing termination condition
nodes.statement: Accordingly, we do not allow the pre-computation procedure of HoD to terminate before the reduced graph $G_i$ has a size no more than $M$. In addition, even after $G_i$ fits in the main memory, we will still continue the preprocessing procedure, until the size of $G_i$ is reduced by less than $5\%$ in an iteration of the processing algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Continue until the reduced graph fits in memory $M$ and an iteration shrinks it by less than 5%.

nodes.name: Memory-fit test
nodes.statement: Accordingly, we do not allow the pre-computation procedure of HoD to terminate before the reduced graph $G_i$ has a size no more than $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Do not stop before the reduced graph fits in $M$

nodes.name: Shrinkage test
nodes.statement: In addition, even after $G_i$ fits in the main memory, we will still continue the preprocessing procedure, until the size of $G_i$ is reduced by less than $5\%$ in an iteration of the processing algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Stop when an iteration shrinks the graph by less than 5%

nodes.name: Index file organization
nodes.statement: Once the preprocessing procedure completes, the core graph $G_c$ is written to the disk in the form of adjacency lists. Meanwhile, the adjacency list of each node not in $G_c$ is separated into two parts that are stored in two different files, $F_f$ and $F_b$. These two files are created at the beginning of HoD's preprocessing algorithm, and they are initially empty. Whenever a node $v$ is removed from the reduced graph $G_i$, we inspect the adjacency list of $v$ in $G_i$, and we append all of $v$'s outgoing (resp.\ incoming) edges to $F_f$ (resp.\ $F_b$). Upon termination of the preprocessing procedure, we reverse the order of nodes in $F_b$, but retain the order of nodes in $F_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $G_c$ as adjacency lists; append each removed node's out-edges to $F_f$ and in-edges to $F_b$; finally reverse $F_b$.

nodes.name: Write core graph
nodes.statement: Once the preprocessing procedure completes, the core graph $G_c$ is written to the disk in the form of adjacency lists.
nodes.statement_short: Store $G_c$ on disk

nodes.name: Create split files
nodes.statement: Meanwhile, the adjacency list of each node not in $G_c$ is separated into two parts that are stored in two different files, $F_f$ and $F_b$. These two files are created at the beginning of HoD's preprocessing algorithm, and they are initially empty.
nodes.statement_short: Create empty files $F_f$, $F_b$

nodes.name: Append edges on removal
nodes.statement: Whenever a node $v$ is removed from the reduced graph $G_i$, we inspect the adjacency list of $v$ in $G_i$, and we append all of $v$'s outgoing (resp.\ incoming) edges to $F_f$ (resp.\ $F_b$).
nodes.statement_short: Append removed node's out/in edges to $F_f$/$F_b$

nodes.name: Reverse backward file
nodes.statement: Upon termination of the preprocessing procedure, we reverse the order of nodes in $F_b$, but retain the order of nodes in $F_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse node order in $F_b$

nodes.name: Forward graph $G_f$
nodes.statement: We refer to the graph represented by $F_f$ as the {\em forward graph}, denoted as $G_f$.

nodes.name: Backward graph $G_b$
nodes.statement: Meanwhile, we refer to the graph represented by $F_b$ as the {\em backward graph}, denoted as $G_b$.

nodes.name: Rank order of $G_f$ and $G_b$
nodes.statement: First, all nodes in $G_f$ (resp.\ $G_b$) are stored in ascending (resp.\ descending) order of their ranks.
conclusions: all nodes in $G_f$ (resp.\ $G_b$) are stored in ascending (resp.\ descending) order of their ranks

nodes.name: Proof of rank order of $G_f$, $G_b$
nodes.statement: To explain this, recall that any node $v$ removed in the $i$-th iteration of the preprocessing algorithm has a rank $r(v)=i$. Consequently, if a node $u$ is stored in $G_f$ before another node $w$, then $r(u) \le r(w)$. As for $G_b$, since we reverse the order of all edges in $G_b$ upon termination of the preprocessing produce, we have $r(u) \ge r(w)$ for any node $u$ that precedes another node $w$ in $G_b$.
nodes.statement_short: Nodes are appended in removal-iteration order, which is rank order; reversing $F_b$ gives descending order.

nodes.name: Edges of $G_f$, $G_b$ go to strictly higher ranks
nodes.statement: Second, for any node $v$, its edges in $G_f$ and $G_b$ only connect it to the nodes whose ranks are strictly higher than $v$.
conclusions: its edges in $G_f$ and $G_b$ only connect it to the nodes whose ranks are strictly higher than $v$

nodes.name: Proof that $G_f$/$G_b$ edges go upward in rank
nodes.statement: This is because, by the time $v$ is removed from the reduced graph, all nodes that rank lower than $v$ must have been eliminated from the reduced graph, and hence, any edge in $v$'s adjacency list only links $v$ to the nodes whose rank is at least $r(v)$. Meanwhile, any neighbor $u$ of $v$ in the reduced graph should have a rank higher than $r(v)$. Otherwise, we have $r(u) = r(v)$, which, by the definition of node ranks, indicates that $u$ and $v$ are removed in the same iteration of the preprocessing algorithm. This is impossible as the pre-computation procedure of HoD never eliminates two adjacent nodes in the same iteration, as explained in Section~\ref{sec:pre-removal}.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-rank nodes are gone when $v$ is removed; an equal-rank neighbor would mean two adjacent nodes removed together, which never happens.

nodes.name: Neighbors have rank at least $r(v)$
nodes.statement: This is because, by the time $v$ is removed from the reduced graph, all nodes that rank lower than $v$ must have been eliminated from the reduced graph, and hence, any edge in $v$'s adjacency list only links $v$ to the nodes whose rank is at least $r(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-rank nodes already removed

nodes.name: Exclude equal rank
nodes.statement: Meanwhile, any neighbor $u$ of $v$ in the reduced graph should have a rank higher than $r(v)$. Otherwise, we have $r(u) = r(v)$, which, by the definition of node ranks, indicates that $u$ and $v$ are removed in the same iteration of the preprocessing algorithm. This is impossible as the pre-computation procedure of HoD never eliminates two adjacent nodes in the same iteration, as explained in Section~\ref{sec:pre-removal}.
nodes.statement_short: Equal rank would mean adjacent nodes removed together, impossible

nodes.name: Preprocessing memory $O(n)$
nodes.statement: The preprocessing algorithm of HoD requires $O(n)$ main memory, where $n$ is the number of nodes in $G$.
assumptions: $n$ is the number of nodes in $G$
conclusions: The preprocessing algorithm of HoD requires $O(n)$ main memory

nodes.name: Argument for $O(n)$ preprocessing memory
nodes.statement: This is because (i) when removing a node $v$ from the reduced graph, HoD needs to record the neighbors of $v$ and exclude them from the node removal process, and (ii) $v$ may have $O(n)$ neighbors. Other parts of the preprocessing algorithm do not have a significant memory requirement.
nodes.statement_short: Only the neighbor set of a removed node, of size $O(n)$, must be held in memory.

nodes.name: Preprocessing I/O and CPU cost
nodes.statement: The major I/O and CPU costs of the preprocessing algorithm are incurred by sorting the edge triplets in each iteration. In the worst case when the input graph $G$ is a complete graph, there are $O(n^2)$ triplets generated in each iteration, leading to a prohibitive I/O and CPU overhead. Fortunately, real-world graphs are seldom complete graphs, and they tend to contain a large number of nodes with small degrees. In that case, each iteration of HoD's preprocessing procedure would only generates a moderate number of edge triplets, leading to a relatively small overhead.
nodes.statement_short: Sorting triplets dominates; worst case $O(n^2)$ triplets per iteration on complete graphs, but small on sparse real graphs.

nodes.name: Index space $O(n^2)$
nodes.statement: Lastly, the space consumption of HoD's index is $O(n^2)$ since, in the worst case, HoD may construct a shortcut from each node $v$ to every node that ranks higher than $v$.
conclusions: the space consumption of HoD's index is $O(n^2)$

nodes.name: HoD PPD query algorithm
nodes.statement: Suppose that we are given a PPD query from a source node $s$ to a destination node $t$. If both $s$ and $t$ are in the core graph $G_c$, then HoD first reads $G_c$ into the main memory, and then answers the query using an in-memory algorithm. On the other hand, if $s$ or $t$ is not in $G_c$, then the algorithm for processing the query is more sophisticated. In particular, in the most challenging case when neither $s$ nor $t$ is in $G_c$, HoD processes the query in three steps: \begin{enumerate} \item {\bf Forward Search:} HoD traverses the forward graph $G_f$ starting from $s$, and for each node $v$ visited, computes the distance from $s$ to $v$ in $G_f$. \item {\bf Backward Search:} This step is similar to the forward search, except that the graph being traversed is $G_b$, and the starting point of the traversal is $t$. \item {\bf Core Search:} Given the distance information obtained in the first two steps, HoD loads the core graph $G_c$ into the main memory, and then derives the distance from $s$ to $t$. \end{enumerate}
input: a PPD query from a source node $s$ to a destination node $t$
nodes.statement_short: For $s,t$ outside the core: forward search in $G_f$ from $s$, backward search in $G_b$ from $t$, then bidirectional core search in memory.

nodes.name: Both endpoints in core
nodes.statement: If both $s$ and $t$ are in the core graph $G_c$, then HoD first reads $G_c$ into the main memory, and then answers the query using an in-memory algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: If $s,t\in G_c$ answer in memory

nodes.name: Forward search
nodes.statement: {\bf Forward Search:} HoD traverses the forward graph $G_f$ starting from $s$, and for each node $v$ visited, computes the distance from $s$ to $v$ in $G_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward search in $G_f$ from $s$

nodes.name: Backward search
nodes.statement: {\bf Backward Search:} This step is similar to the forward search, except that the graph being traversed is $G_b$, and the starting point of the traversal is $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Backward search in $G_b$ from $t$

nodes.name: Core search
nodes.statement: {\bf Core Search:} Given the distance information obtained in the first two steps, HoD loads the core graph $G_c$ into the main memory, and then derives the distance from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Core search in memory derives $dist(s,t)$

nodes.name: Index value $\theta(v)$
nodes.statement: For convenience, we define an {\em index} value $\theta(v)$ for each node {\em not} in the core graph $G_c$, such that $\theta(v) = i$ only if the $i$-th adjacency list in $G_f$ belongs to $v$.

nodes.name: Index order respects rank
nodes.statement: By the way $G_f$ is constructed (see Section~\ref{sec:pre-terminate}), for any two nodes $u$ and $v$ with $\theta(u) < \theta(v)$, the rank of $u$ is no larger than the rank of $v$.
assumptions: for any two nodes $u$ and $v$ with $\theta(u) < \theta(v)$
conclusions: the rank of $u$ is no larger than the rank of $v$

nodes.name: HoD forward search
nodes.statement: The forward search of HoD maintains a hash table $H_f$ and a min-heap $Q_f$. In particular, $H_f$ maps each node $v$ to a key $\kappa_f(v)$, which equals the length of the shortest path from $s$ to $v$ that is seen so far. Initially, $\kappa_f(s) = 0$, and $\kappa_f(v) = +\infty$ for any node $v \ne s$. On the other hand, each entry in $Q_f$ corresponds to a node $v$, and the key of the entry equals $\theta(v)$, i.e., the index of $v$. As will become evident shortly, $Q_f$ ensures that the forward search visits nodes in ascending order of their indices, and hence, it scans the file structure of $G_f$ only once, without the need to backtrack to any disk block that it has visited before. HoD starts the forward search by inspecting each edge $e = \langle s, v\rangle$ adjacent to $s$ in $G_f$, and then inserting $v$ into $H_f$ with a key $\kappa(v) = l(e)$. (Note that $G_f$ contains only outgoing edges.) In addition, HoD also inserts $v$ into $Q_f$. After that, HoD iteratively removes the top entry $u$ in $Q_f$, and processes $u$ as follows: for each edge $e = \langle u, v\rangle$ adjacent to $u$, if $\kappa_f(v) = +\infty$ in the hash table $H_f$, HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \kappa_f(u) + l(e)$ and inserts $v$ into $Q_f$; otherwise, if HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \min\{\kappa_f(v), \kappa_f(u) + l(e)\}$. When $Q_f$ becomes empty, HoD terminates the forward search, and retains the hash table $H_f$ for the third step of the algorithm, i.e., the core search.
nodes.statement_short: Index-ordered Dijkstra-like scan of $G_f$ from $s$ with heap keyed by $\theta$, relaxing outgoing edges; one pass over the file.

nodes.name: Initialize hash table and heap
nodes.statement: The forward search of HoD maintains a hash table $H_f$ and a min-heap $Q_f$. In particular, $H_f$ maps each node $v$ to a key $\kappa_f(v)$, which equals the length of the shortest path from $s$ to $v$ that is seen so far. nodes.statement_short: $Q_f$ ordered by index, giving a single file scan

nodes.name: Expand source
nodes.statement: HoD starts the forward search by inspecting each edge $e = \langle s, v\rangle$ adjacent to $s$ in $G_f$, and then inserting $v$ into $H_f$ with a key $\kappa(v) = l(e)$. (Note that $G_f$ contains only outgoing edges.) In addition, HoD also inserts $v$ into $Q_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Insert out-neighbors of $s$

nodes.name: Process heap top
nodes.statement: After that, HoD iteratively removes the top entry $u$ in $Q_f$, and processes $u$ as follows: for each edge $e = \langle u, v\rangle$ adjacent to $u$, if $\kappa_f(v) = +\infty$ in the hash table $H_f$, HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \kappa_f(u) + l(e)$ and inserts $v$ into $Q_f$; otherwise, if HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \min\{\kappa_f(v), \kappa_f(u) + l(e)\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pop lowest-index node and relax its edges

nodes.name: Terminate
nodes.statement: When $Q_f$ becomes empty, HoD terminates the forward search, and retains the hash table $H_f$ for the third step of the algorithm, i.e., the core search.
nodes.statement_short: Stop when $Q_f$ empty; keep $H_f$

nodes.name: HoD backward search (PPD)
nodes.statement: The backward search of HoD works in a manner very similar to the forward search, and it also maintains a hash table $H_b$ and a min-heap $Q_b$. $H_b$ maps each node $v$ to a key $\kappa_b(v)$, while $Q_b$ sorts nodes according to their index values. When the backward search starts, HoD sets $\kappa_b(t) = 0$ and $\kappa_b(v) = +\infty$ for any $v \ne t$, after which it inserts $t$ into $Q_b$. Then, HoD iteratively extracts the top entry $u$ in $Q_b$, and processes $u$ as follows. First, HoD examines the neighbors of $u$ in $G_b$ (recall that $G_b$ only records the incoming edges of each node). For each neighbor $v$, if $\kappa_b(v) = +\infty$ in $H_b$, then HoD adds $v$ into $Q_b$, setting $\kappa_b(v)$ to the length of the edge $\langle u, v \rangle$; otherwise, if $\kappa_b(v) > \kappa_b(u) + l(\langle u, v \rangle)$, then HoD updates $\kappa_b(v)$ to $\kappa_b(u) + l(\langle u, v \rangle)$. The backward search completes when $Q_b$ is empty, upon which HoD retrieves the hash table $H_b$ and moves on to the core search.
nodes.statement_short: Mirror of the forward search on $G_b$ from $t$, computing upper bounds $\kappa_b(v)$ on distances to $t$.

nodes.name: Initialize
nodes.statement: The backward search of HoD works in a manner very similar to the forward search, and it also maintains a hash table $H_b$ and a min-heap $Q_b$. $H_b$ maps each node $v$ to a key $\kappa_b(v)$, while $Q_b$ sorts nodes according to their index values. When the backward search starts, HoD sets $\kappa_b(t) = 0$ and $\kappa_b(v) = +\infty$ for any $v \ne t$, after which it inserts $t$ into $Q_b$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up $H_b$, $Q_b$ with $\kappa_b(t)=0$

nodes.name: Process heap top
nodes.statement: Then, HoD iteratively extracts the top entry $u$ in $Q_b$, and processes $u$ as follows. First, HoD examines the neighbors of $u$ in $G_b$ (recall that $G_b$ only records the incoming edges of each node). For each neighbor $v$, if $\kappa_b(v) = +\infty$ in $H_b$, then HoD adds $v$ into $Q_b$, setting $\kappa_b(v)$ to the length of the edge $\langle u, v \rangle$; otherwise, if $\kappa_b(v) > \kappa_b(u) + l(\langle u, v \rangle)$, then HoD updates $\kappa_b(v)$ to $\kappa_b(u) + l(\langle u, v \rangle)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pop and relax incoming edges

nodes.name: Terminate
nodes.statement: The backward search completes when $Q_b$ is empty, upon which HoD retrieves the hash table $H_b$ and moves on to the core search.
nodes.statement_short: Stop when $Q_b$ empty

nodes.name: HoD core search (PPD)
nodes.statement: The core search of HoD performs two traversals of the core graph $G_c$, and the first (resp.\ second) traversal is essentially a continuation of the forward (resp.\ backward) search. In particular, the core search uses the hash tables $H_f$ and $H_b$ created during the forward and backward searches, along with two new min-heaps $\QFF$ and $\QBB$. Each entry in $\QFF$ (resp.\ $\QBB$) corresponds to a node $v$, and the key of the entry equals the value $\kappa_f(v)$ in $H_f$ (resp.\ $\kappa_b(v)$ in $H_b$). This contrasts the forward and backward searches, which uses min-heaps where the key of each entry is the index value of a node. In addition, HoD also maintains a variable $\dm$ that records the smallest distance from $s$ to $t$ in the part of the augmented graph that has been traversed. Initially, $\dm = \min_v \big\{\kappa_f(v) + \kappa_b(v)\big\}$. (Observe that $\kappa_f(v)$ is an upper-bound of the distance from $s$ to $v$ and $\kappa_b(v)$ is an upper-bound of the distance from $v$ to $t$.) As the first step of the core search, HoD inserts into $\QFF$ any node $u \in G_c$ with $\kappa_f(u) \ne +\infty$ (i.e., $u$ is reached by the forward search previously). Similarly, it also adds into $\QBB$ any node $w \in G_c$ with $\kappa_b(u) \ne +\infty$. After that, HoD removes the top entries from $\QFF$ and $\QBB$ in a round-robin fashion. Whenever it extracts an entry $u$ from $\QFF$, it inspects both $\kappa_f(u)$ and $\kappa_b(u)$. If $\kappa_f(u) + \kappa_b(u) < \dm$, then HoD sets $\dm = \kappa_f(u)+\kappa_b(u)$. In addition, for each outgoing edge $e = \langle u, v\rangle$ from $u$, HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \min\{\kappa_f(v), \kappa_f(u) + l(e)\}$, and inserts $v$ into $\QFF$ (if $v$ has not been inserted before). The core search terminates when $\dm$ is smaller than or equal to $\kappa_f(u) + \kappa_b(w)$, where $u$ and $w$ are the top entries in $\QFF$ and $\QBB$, respectively. The rationale is that, for any unseen entry $v$, the distance from $s$ to $v$ is at least $\kappa_f(u)$, and the distance from $v$ to $t$ is at least $\kappa_b(w)$. As a consequence, if $\dm \le \kappa_f(u) + \kappa_b(w)$, then the path from $s$ to $t$ via $v$ cannot be shorter than $\dm$. Upon termination of the core search, HoD returns $\dm$ as the result of the PPD query from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Bidirectional Dijkstra on the in-memory core graph seeded by $\kappa_f,\kappa_b$, stopping when the best $s$-$t$ distance cannot improve.

nodes.name: Initialize heaps and best distance
nodes.statement: In particular, the core search uses the hash tables $H_f$ and $H_b$ created during the forward and backward searches, along with two new min-heaps $\QFF$ and $\QBB$. nodes.name: Seed heaps

Whenever it extracts an entry $u$ from $\QFF$, it inspects both $\kappa_f(u)$ and $\kappa_b(u)$. If $\kappa_f(u) + \kappa_b(u) < \dm$, then HoD sets $\dm = \kappa_f(u)+\kappa_b(u)$. nodes.name: Termination test
nodes.statement: The core search terminates when $\dm$ is smaller than or equal to $\kappa_f(u) + \kappa_b(w)$, where $u$ and $w$ are the top entries in $\QFF$ and $\QBB$, respectively. nodes.name: Return result
nodes.statement: Upon termination of the core search, HoD returns $\dm$ as the result of the PPD query from $s$ to $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Return best distance

nodes.name: Degenerate PPD cases
nodes.statement: The above discussion assumes that neither $s$ or $t$ is in the core graph $G_c$. Nevertheless, HoD can easily handle the case when $s$ or $t$ is in $G_c$. In particular, if $s$ is in $G_c$, then HoD simply omits the forward search. Accordingly, the core search will use a hash table $H_f$ where $\kappa_f(s) = 0$ and $\kappa_f(v) = +\infty$ for every $v \ne s$. The case when $t$ is not in $G_c$ is handled similarly.
nodes.statement_short: If $s$ (or $t$) is in the core, skip the corresponding search and seed the core search with $\kappa_f(s)=0$.

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (PPD correctness)
nodes.statement: Given any source node $s$ and any destination node $t$, HoD correctly computes the distance from $s$ to $t$.
assumptions: Given any source node $s$ and any destination node $t$
conclusions: HoD correctly computes the distance from $s$ to $t$
nodes.label: lmm:p2p-correct

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Let $v_i$ ($i \ge 1$) be the node in $G_f$ with the $i$-th largest index value. We define $S_0$ as the set of nodes in $G_c$, and $S_i$ ($i \ge 1$) as a set that contains all nodes in $G_c$ as well as $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_i$. We will use an induction on $i$ to show that, for any $S_i$, HoD can correctly compute the distance between any two nodes in $S_i$. Consider the base case when $i = 0$. When both $s$ and $t$ are in $S_0$, HoD computes the distance from $s$ to $t$ based only on the nodes and edges in $G_c$. Recall that, in the preprocessing procedure of HoD, whenever we remove a node from the reduced graph, we always construct shortcuts between the remaining nodes, to ensure that the distance between any two remaining nodes is not affected. Therefore, the distance from $s$ to $t$ in $G_c$ should be equal to $dist(s, t)$, i.e., HoD should return correct result for the PPD query. Assume that HoD can correctly compute the distance between any two nodes in $S_i$ ($i \ge 0$). Let $u$ be the node in $S_{i+1}$ but not $S_i$. We will first prove that HoD can correctly derive the distance from $u$ to any other node $v$ in $S_{i+1}$. First, since $v \in S_{i+1}$ and $v \ne u$, $v$ must be in $S_i$. Let $P$ be the shortest path from $u$ to $v$ in the original graph. Among the nodes in $S_i$ that also appear on $P$, let $w$ be the one that minimizes $dist(u, w)$. By the preprocessing algorithm of HoD, the distance from $u$ to $w$ should be preserved in the reduced graph, when all nodes not in $S_{i+1}$ are removed. This indicates that $u$ should have a shortcut to $w$, and the shortcut should have a length $dist(u, w)$. Therefore, when HoD performs the forward search from $u$, it can correctly identify the distance from $u$ to $w$. Meanwhile, by the induction hypothesis, HoD can also derive the correct distance from $w$ to $v$. Therefore, the distance from $u$ to $v$ can be correctly calculated by HoD. In a similar manner, we can also show that HoD can return the correct distance from any other node $v \in S_{i+1}$ to $u$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of non-core nodes added to the core node set, in decreasing index order. The inductive step uses that the shortcut from $u$ to the nearest node $w\in S_i$ on its shortest path has length $dist(u,w)$.

nodes.statement: This is because, during the core search, the algorithm reads $G_c$ into the memory, and it needs to maintain two hash tables and two min-heaps, each of which takes $O(n)$ space.
nodes.statement_short: Core graph plus two hash tables and two heaps of size $O(n)$.

nodes.name: Argument for PPD query time
nodes.statement: When processing a query, HoD inserts each node into each min-heap at most once, and it visits each edge in $G_c$, $G_f$, and $G_b$ no more than once.
nodes.statement_short: Each node enters each heap once and each edge is visited once.

assumptions: $m'$ is the total number of edges in $G_c$, $G_f$, and $G_b$

nodes.name: HoD SSD query algorithm
nodes.statement: Given an SSD query from a node $s$ that is not in the core graph $G_c$, HoD processes the query in three steps: \begin{enumerate}[itemsep = 0.5mm, topsep = 2mm] \item {\bf Forward Search:} HoD traverses the forward graph $G_f$ starting from $s$, and for each node $v$ visited, computes the distance from $s$ to $v$ in $G_f$. \item {\bf Core Search:} HoD reads the core graph $G_c$ into the main memory, and continues the forward search by following the outgoing edges of each node in $G_c$. \item {\bf Backward Search:} HoD linearly scans the backward graph $G_b$ to derive the exact distance from $s$ to any node not in $G_c$. \end{enumerate} On the other hand, if $s$ is in $G_c$, then HoD would answer the query with a core search followed by a backward search, skipping the forward search.
input: an SSD query from a node $s$
nodes.statement_short: Forward search in $G_f$, Dijkstra continuation on the in-memory core graph, then one sequential scan of $G_b$ relaxing incoming edges.

nodes.name: Forward search
nodes.statement: {\bf Forward Search:} HoD traverses the forward graph $G_f$ starting from $s$, and for each node $v$ visited, computes the distance from $s$ to $v$ in $G_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward search in $G_f$ from $s$

nodes.name: Core search
nodes.statement: {\bf Core Search:} HoD reads the core graph $G_c$ into the main memory, and continues the forward search by following the outgoing edges of each node in $G_c$.
nodes.statement_short: Continue search in in-memory core graph

nodes.name: Backward search
nodes.statement: {\bf Backward Search:} HoD linearly scans the backward graph $G_b$ to derive the exact distance from $s$ to any node not in $G_c$.
nodes.statement_short: Linear scan of $G_b$ for exact distances

nodes.name: Source in core
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $s$ is in $G_c$, then HoD would answer the query with a core search followed by a backward search, skipping the forward search.

nodes.name: HoD core search (SSD)
nodes.statement: The core search of HoD is a continuation of the forward search, and it inherits the hash table $H_f$ created during the forward search. In addition to $H_f$, HoD creates a min-heap $Q_c$, such that $Q_c$ stores entries of the form $\langle v, \kappa_f(v)\rangle$, where $v$ is a node and $\kappa_f(v)$ is the key of $v$ in $H_f$. For any node $u$ with $\kappa_f(u) \ne +\infty$ (i.e., $u$ is visited by the forward search), HoD inserts $u$ into $Q_c$. Given $H_f$ and $Q_c$, HoD performs the core search in iterations. In each iteration, HoD extracts the top entry $v$ from $Q_c$, and examines each outgoing edge $e$ of $v$. For every such edge, HoD inspects its ending point $w$, and sets $\kappa_f(w) = \min\{\kappa_f(w), \kappa_f(v) + l(e)\}$. Then, HoD adds $w$ into $Q_c$ if $w$ is currently not in $Q_c$. This iterative procedure is repeated until $Q_c$ becomes empty. After that, the hash table $H_f$ is sent to the last step (i.e., the backward search) for further processing.
nodes.statement_short: Dijkstra on the core graph seeded with all nodes reached by the forward search.

nodes.name: Seed heap
nodes.statement: The core search of HoD is a continuation of the forward search, and it inherits the hash table $H_f$ created during the forward search. In addition to $H_f$, HoD creates a min-heap $Q_c$, such that $Q_c$ stores entries of the form $\langle v, \kappa_f(v)\rangle$, where $v$ is a node and $\kappa_f(v)$ is the key of $v$ in $H_f$. For any node $u$ with $\kappa_f(u) \ne +\infty$ (i.e., $u$ is visited by the forward search), HoD inserts $u$ into $Q_c$.
nodes.statement_short: Create $Q_c$ and insert all reached nodes

nodes.name: Dijkstra iterations
nodes.statement: Given $H_f$ and $Q_c$, HoD performs the core search in iterations. In each iteration, HoD extracts the top entry $v$ from $Q_c$, and examines each outgoing edge $e$ of $v$. For every such edge, HoD inspects its ending point $w$, and sets $\kappa_f(w) = \min\{\kappa_f(w), \kappa_f(v) + l(e)\}$. Then, HoD adds $w$ into $Q_c$ if $w$ is currently not in $Q_c$. This iterative procedure is repeated until $Q_c$ becomes empty.
nodes.statement_short: Pop top node, relax outgoing edges, repeat

nodes.name: Pass hash table on
nodes.statement: After that, the hash table $H_f$ is sent to the last step (i.e., the backward search) for further processing.
nodes.statement_short: Hand $H_f$ to backward search

nodes.name: HoD backward search (SSD)
nodes.statement: Given the hash table $H_f$ obtained from the core search, the reversed search of HoD is performed as a sequential scan of the backward graph $G_b$, which stores nodes in descending order of their index values. For each node $v$ visited during the sequential scan, HoD checks each edge $e = \langle u, v\rangle$ adjacent to $v$. (Note that $G_b$ contains only incoming edges). If $\kappa_f(u) \ne +\infty$ and $\kappa_f(u) + l(e) < \kappa_f(v)$, then HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \kappa_f(u) + l(e)$. Once all nodes in $G_b$ are scanned, HoD terminates the backward search and, for each node $v$, returns $\kappa_f(v)$ as the distance from $s$ to $v$.
nodes.statement_short: Sequential scan of $G_b$ in descending index order, relaxing each node's incoming edges; no heap needed.

nodes.name: Sequential scan
nodes.statement: Given the hash table $H_f$ obtained from the core search, the reversed search of HoD is performed as a sequential scan of the backward graph $G_b$, which stores nodes in descending order of their index values.
nodes.statement_short: Scan $G_b$ sequentially

nodes.name: Relax incoming edges
nodes.statement: For each node $v$ visited during the sequential scan, HoD checks each edge $e = \langle u, v\rangle$ adjacent to $v$. (Note that $G_b$ contains only incoming edges). If $\kappa_f(u) \ne +\infty$ and $\kappa_f(u) + l(e) < \kappa_f(v)$, then HoD sets $\kappa_f(v) = \kappa_f(u) + l(e)$.
nodes.statement_short: Relax each incoming edge

nodes.name: Return distances
nodes.statement: Once all nodes in $G_b$ are scanned, HoD terminates the backward search and, for each node $v$, returns $\kappa_f(v)$ as the distance from $s$ to $v$.
nodes.statement_short: Return $\kappa_f$ values

nodes.name: Heap-free backward search
nodes.statement: One interesting fact about the backward search is that it does not require a heap to decide the order in which the nodes are visited. This leads to a much smaller CPU cost compared with Dijkstra's algorithm, as it avoids all expensive heap operations.

nodes.statement: Given a source node $s$, the SSD query algorithm of HoD returns $dist(s, v)$ for each node $v \in G$.
conclusions: the SSD query algorithm of HoD returns $dist(s, v)$ for each node $v \in G$

nodes.name: HoD extension for SSSP queries
nodes.statement: To extend HoD for SSSP queries, we associate each edge $\langle u, w\rangle$ in the augment graph $G^*$ with a node $v$, such that $v$ immediately precedes $w$ on the shortest path from $u$ to $w$ in $G$. For example, given the augmented graph in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}e, we would associate the edge $\langle v_9, v_7\rangle$ with $v_6$, since (i) the shortest path from $v_9$ to $v_7$ in $G$ is $\langle v_9, v_6, v_7\rangle$, and (ii) $v_6$ immediately precedes $v_7$ in the path. With the above extension, HoD processes any SSSP query from a node $s$ using the algorithm for SSD query with one modification: Whenever HoD traverses an edge $\langle u, w\rangle$ and finds that $dist(s, u) + l(\langle u, w \rangle) < dist(s, w)$, HoD would not only update $dist(s, w)$ but also record the node associated with $\langle u, w\rangle$. That is, for each node $w$ visited, HoD keeps track of the predecessor of $w$ in the shortest path from $s$ to $w$ that have been seen so far. As such, when the SSD query algorithm terminates, HoD can immediately return $dist(s, w)$ as well as the predecessor of $w$. Finally, we clarify how the preprocessing algorithm of HoD can be extended to derive the node associated with each edge. First, for each edge $e$ in the original graph, HoD associates $e$ with the starting point of $e$. After that, whenever HoD generates a candidate edge $\langle u, w\rangle$ during the removal of a node $v$, HoD would associate $\langle u, w\rangle$ with the node that is associated with the edge $\langle v, w\rangle$. For example, in Figure~\ref{fig:over-steps}c, when HoD removes $v_7$ and creates a candidate edge $\langle v_9, v_{10}\rangle$, it associates the edge with $v_7$, which is the node associated with $\langle v_7, v_{10}\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Annotate each edge with the predecessor of its head on the underlying shortest path; record it during relaxations to output predecessors.

nodes.name: Remark on using largest connected components
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark.} The previous experimental study on VC-Index \cite{ckcc12} uses USRN, u-BTC, and u-UKWeb instead of their largest connected components (CC) for experiments. We do not follow this approach as it leads to less meaningful results. To explain, consider a massive undirected graph $G$ where each CC is small enough to fit in the main-memory. On such a graph, even if a disk-based method can efficiently answer SSD queries, it does not necessarily mean that it is more scalable than a main-memory algorithm. In particular, one can easily answer an SSD query from any node $s$ in $G$, by first reading into memory the CC that contains $s$, and then running a main-memory SSD algorithm on the CC. In general, given any graph $G$, one can use an I/O efficient algorithm \cite{mr99} to pre-compute the (weakly) connected components in $G$, and then handle SSD queries on each component separately.
nodes.statement_short: Testing on graphs whose components fit in memory is uninformative, so experiments use the largest (weakly) connected component.

nodes.statement: The majority of those algorithms focus on two types of queries: (i) {\em point-to-point shortest path (PPSP)} queries, which ask for the shortest path from one node to another, and (ii) {\em point-to-point distance (PPD)} queries, which ask for the length of the shortest path between two given nodes.
nodes.statement_short: PPSP: shortest path between two nodes; PPD: its length.

nodes.name: SSD via $n$ PPD queries
nodes.statement: These two types of queries are closely related to SSD and SSSP queries, in the sense that any SSD (resp.\ SSSP) query can be answered using the results of $n$ PPD (resp.\ PPSP) queries, where $n$ is the number of nodes in the graph.
